questions.prompt: A patient's blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Approximately what is the mean arterial pressure?
questions.explanation: MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓ × (systolic − diastolic) = 80 + ⅓ × 40 ≈ 93 mmHg. The mean sits nearer diastolic because diastole lasts longer than systole at normal heart rates.
questions.learning_objective: Estimate mean arterial pressure from systolic and diastolic pressures.

questions.prompt: When a healthy person stands up quickly from lying down, what does the baroreceptor reflex do?

choices.a: Nothing: blood pressure doesn't change on standing
choices.c: Less baroreceptor firing: sympathetic output rises and vagal tone falls, raising heart rate and vascular resistance
choices.d: More baroreceptor firing: the heart rate slows

questions.explanation: Standing pools blood in the legs, reducing venous return, stroke volume and pressure. The carotid and aortic baroreceptors fire less, so the brainstem increases sympathetic and reduces vagal outflow: heart rate, contractility and arteriolar tone rise within seconds.
questions.learning_objective: Describe the baroreceptor response to standing.

questions.prompt: On repeated, properly measured readings, a 45-year-old's average blood pressure is 136/84 mmHg. Under the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline, this is:
questions.explanation: Stage 1 hypertension is a systolic of 130–139 or a diastolic of 80–89 mmHg. Elevated is 120–129 with diastolic below 80; stage 2 is 140 or more systolic, or 90 or more diastolic.
questions.learning_objective: Classify blood pressure readings using the 2017 ACC/AHA categories.

questions.prompt: Two months after starting lisinopril, a patient has a persistent dry cough with a clear chest. What is the best change?

choices.b: Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker, such as losartan
choices.c: Switch to a higher dose of lisinopril
choices.d: Add a cough suppressant and continue lisinopril

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors reduce the breakdown of bradykinin, which causes a dry cough in a minority of patients. Angiotensin receptor blockers block the effect of angiotensin II at its receptor without raising bradykinin, so the cough usually resolves.
questions.learning_objective: Manage ACE-inhibitor cough by switching to an ARB.

questions.prompt: Which antihypertensive should be stopped in a woman who is planning pregnancy?

choices.c: An ACE inhibitor (or an angiotensin receptor blocker)

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic, especially in the second and third trimesters (fetal kidney damage, oligohydramnios). Labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa are used in pregnancy.

questions.prompt: Which change makes the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney release more renin?

choices.b: Reduced perfusion pressure in the afferent arteriole
choices.c: High blood pressure in the renal artery
choices.d: High sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa

questions.explanation: Renin release rises with low afferent arteriolar pressure, low NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa, and sympathetic (β1) stimulation. Angiotensin II feeds back to suppress it.
questions.learning_objective: List the stimuli for renin release.

questions.prompt: Three weeks after starting hydrochlorothiazide, a man has a hot, swollen, painful big-toe joint. How did the drug likely contribute?

choices.a: Thiazides raise serum uric acid, which can precipitate gout.
choices.b: Thiazides cause a drug allergy limited to the toe.
choices.c: Thiazides lower uric acid too quickly.
choices.d: Thiazides cause hypercalcemia, which crystallizes in joints.

questions.explanation: Thiazides reduce urate excretion (they compete for secretion in the proximal tubule and cause volume contraction), raising serum urate and the risk of gout attacks. Other effects: low K⁺ and Na⁺, high Ca²⁺ and glucose.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize hyperuricemia and gout as adverse effects of thiazides.
